title: The Easiest Method for Memorizing the Noble Qur'an

paragraphs: Chapter One: The Noble Qur'an
Section One: The Status of the Qur'an
The great Qur'an is the best and most excellent of the revealed books.

1 — The speech of Allah is the finest of speech, and the excellence of His speech over the speech of creation is like the excellence of the Creator over the created. The Prophets before it were given glad tidings of it prior to its revelation.
2 — Allah, glorified be He, praised His own Sacred Self for sending down the Qur'an. He swore by the Wise Qur'an and ordained for it loftiness in itself and in its worth.

3 — He conferred it as a favor upon this nation: a Messenger from among them recites His verses, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom. He mentioned teaching the Qur'an first, ahead of many of His blessings.
The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an, created man, and taught him clear expression.
Section Two: The Attributes of the Qur'an
Allah described the Qur'an with magnificent attributes.
1 — Mighty (ʿazīz): nothing rivals it in its might, and whoever draws near to it attains might.
2 — Possessed of majesty and standing, characterized by the perfection of greatness.
3 — Glorious (majīd), abounding in worldly and otherworldly noble qualities.
4 — Noble (karīm), having reached the highest degree of honor.
5 — Wise (ḥakīm), and in it is wisdom.
6 — Blessed (mubārak), abounding in good and in benefits.
7 — Clear in its wording and its meaning, and a clarification of matters as they truly are. Ibn Masʿūd said: “Every knowledge and every matter has been made clear for us in this Qur'an.”
Section Three: The Inimitability of the Qur'an
1 — The Noble Qur'an is a book that nothing equals.
2 — The Noble Qur'an is the best of discourse. Its verses resemble one another in truth and beauty, and the skins and hearts of those who fear their Lord soften at its remembrance.

3 — It encompasses all the sciences and the most beneficial branches of knowledge. In it are the most truthful reports, the clearest proofs and evidences, the finest stories, the most eloquent wisdom, and the most beautiful rhetoric.
4 — The Qur'an has a distinction in its wording and Arabic composition that nothing can match. It is not poetry, rhymed prose, or ordinary address; no speech resembles its order.
5 — Its inimitability in meaning is greater and more abundant than its inimitability in wording. Even if mankind and jinn gathered together, they could not produce its like.

6 — The Book of Allah is comprehensive in its rulings, just in its judgments, and wise in its commands and prohibitions. It carries awe, majesty, force, influence, and beauty. It guides through the easiest indications and no sane person hears it without recognizing its truth.
Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an.
Section Four: The Wisdom Behind the Revelation of the Qur'an
1 — No one can do without the Book of Allah. Our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was the most perfect of people in intellect, yet his guidance came through what his Lord revealed to him.
2 — Allah sent down the Qur'an as an admonition, a healing for what is in the hearts, guidance, and mercy for the believers.
3 — He made it a light for His servants.
4 — It is the foundation of character and noble qualities. When ʿĀʾishah was asked about the character of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, she replied that his character was the Qur'an.
O mankind, there has come to you instruction from your Lord, healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.
Section Five: Rejoicing in the Qur'an
1 — Rejoicing in the great Qur'an is among the loftiest stations of faith. Allah informed us that the People of the Book rejoiced at the revelation sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ.

2 — The rejoicing of this nation in its Book is greater than the rejoicing of others, in compliance with the command of Allah to rejoice in His bounty and mercy. Ibn Kathīr said that this guidance and true religion are more worthy of joy than the vanishing attractions of worldly life.
3 — The happiest of people are those who are nearest to the Book of Allah, for it is a light.
In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy—in that let them rejoice.
Chapter Two: Learning the Noble Qur'an
Section One: Gatherings of the Qur'an

1 — Gatherings of the Qur'an are places in which tranquility and mercy descend. The angels surround those who recite the Book of Allah and study it together, and Allah mentions them among those who are with Him.
2 — The best companions a person can have are the people of the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the reciters—whether mature or young—were the companions of ʿUmar's gatherings and consultation.
3 — The people of the Qur'an who know its meanings are truly the scholars; its verses are clear signs preserved in the breasts of those given knowledge.
4 — Whoever turns to the Qur'an sincerely for Allah, Allah raises him. The Prophet ﷺ said that by this Book Allah raises some people and lowers others.

No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it together, except that tranquility descends upon them, mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and Allah mentions them among those with Him.
Section Two: The Virtue of Learning the Qur'an

1 — Allah taught His servants the Qur'an and made its recitation, understanding, and memorization easy for those upon whom He has mercy. Arab and non-Arab, young and old, male and female, rich and poor all recite and memorize it.
2 — Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl supplicated that Allah send a messenger who would recite His verses and teach the Book and wisdom.
3 — The teacher of the Qur'an and its learner are the best of people.

4 — Learning the Qur'an is better than the wealth of this world. Learning two verses is better than possessing two valuable she-camels, and three or four verses are better than the same number of camels.

5 — The Salaf were keen to teach the Noble Qur'an to children so faith would take root in their hearts. Ibn Khaldūn called teaching children the Qur'an a symbol of the religion and the foundation upon which later abilities are built.

6 — Knowing its virtue, the Salaf held fast to learning even on their journeys. Abū Bakr al-Shadhāʾī accompanied his teacher roughly 847 kilometers from Baghdad to Damascus so that he could continue reciting the Qur'an to him.
The best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it.
Section Three: The Virtue of Reciting the Qur'an
1 — Allah has honored the reciter with abundant reward. Whoever reads one letter from the Book of Allah receives a good deed multiplied tenfold. Alif, lām, and mīm are each a letter.
2 — Recitation of the Qur'an is among the causes of steadfastness. It was revealed gradually to strengthen the heart of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers.
3 — The Qur'an is a proof for its people on the Day of Judgment and an accepted intercessor with the Lord of the worlds.
Recite the Qur'an, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions.
Section Four: The Virtue of Memorizing the Qur'an
1 — The memorizer of the Qur'an is with the noble, righteous angels. The one who recites while finding it difficult receives two rewards.

2 — The counsel of the scholars is to give priority to memorizing the Book of Allah. Ibn al-Jawzī observed that life is precious and knowledge vast, so the most important and excellent knowledge should come first.
3 — The Salaf occupied children with memorizing the Qur'an and hearing Hadith so that faith would be established in their hearts.

4 — Advanced age does not prevent memorization. The revelation was completed when Abū Bakr was sixty-one, yet he memorized the entire Qur'an; Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn Ḥammūyah memorized it at eighty.
5 — Whoever has not memorized anything of the Book of Allah has a heart likened by the Prophet ﷺ to a ruined house.
The one who recites the Qur'an while having memorized it is with the noble and righteous scribes.
Section Five: Reverent Fear When Reciting the Qur'an
1 — The Qur'an is full of admonitions, warnings, and obligations. Had it been sent down upon a mountain, it would have been seen humbled and split asunder out of fear of Allah.

2 — Its verses made the great ones weep. When Ibn Masʿūd recited Sūrat al-Nisāʾ to the Messenger ﷺ, he looked up and saw the Prophet's eyes overflowing with tears. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Shikhkhīr heard a sound from the Prophet's chest in prayer like a boiling pot because of his weeping.

Abū Bakr could not restrain his eyes when reciting. ʿUmar wept during Sūrat Yūsuf until his voice broke. Ibn ʿAbbās recited carefully, letter by letter, with sobbing and drawn-out weeping. The Companions' eyes would fill with tears and their skins shiver when the Qur'an was recited.

Jaʿfar recited part of Sūrat Maryam before the Negus, who wept until his beard was wet; his bishops also wept. When people from Yemen heard the Qur'an in the time of Abū Bakr and began to weep, he said: “This is how we once were, then the hearts hardened.”
Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of Allah.
Section Six: The Station of the Bearer of the Qur'an
1 — The people of the Qur'an are the people of Allah and His elect.
2 — The Book of Allah is mighty; whoever draws near to it, Allah raises his station. A person who had learned al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān was regarded as great among the Companions.

3 — Allah promised the one skilled in the Qur'an that he will be with the noble angels. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ explained that this may mean a station alongside the angelic scribes, because the reciter carries the Book and follows their path.
4 — People of sound opinion take reciters as companions and consult them; the reciters were the companions of ʿUmar's gatherings and consultation.

5 — The bearer is honored in life and after death. The person most versed in the Book leads the prayer, and among the martyrs of Uḥud the Prophet ﷺ placed first in the grave the one who had taken more of the Qur'an.
6 — The bearer of the Qur'an is in the highest degrees of bliss. He will be told to recite, ascend, and recite with measured pace as in the world; his station will be at the last verse he recites.
The people of the Qur'an are the people of Allah and His elect.
Chapter Three: The Easiest Method for Memorizing the Noble Qur'an
Section One: Rules and Guidelines for Memorization
1 — Memorization should be from a standardized printed muṣḥaf, so it helps the firmness of memorization and the speed of recalling the locations of verses and the endings and beginnings of pages.
2 — Your memorization must be under a shaykh, to correct your recitation.
3 — Let your memorization be daily, for interruption weakens resolve and memorization.
4 — The principle in memorization is repetition; the more repetition increases, the more mastered the memorization becomes.
5 — Memorization proceeds from Sūrat al-Nās up to Sūrat al-Baqarah because it is easier. After completing the Qur'an, review proceeds from al-Baqarah to al-Nās.
6 — If time for memorization and review becomes tight, give review precedence over memorization.
7 — Do not move to a new page until you have mastered what precedes it, with no error and no hesitation.

8 — During the first two years, every memorizer finds some of what was memorized slipping away. This is the consolidation stage. Do not grieve over mistakes or let Satan's whispering hold you back. Continue, for the Qur'an is a treasure not given to just anyone.
Section Two: The Daily Amount of Memorization

1 — Memorize one page each day. If your memorization is mastered, you may increase beyond one page. If you take on too much without mastery, what is memorized will be weak. If you are unable to memorize a page daily, memorize what you are able.
2 — Do not increase in a single day beyond two pages, lest the material pile up and slip away; whoever memorizes quickly forgets quickly.
Section Three: The Method of Memorizing the Qur'an
There are many methods for memorizing the Noble Qur'an. The author presents one distinguished by speed, strength, and mastery, illustrated with one page from Sūrat al-Jumuʿah.
First, read the whole page correctly while looking at the text to your teacher until you master its reading. Then divide the page into two halves.

Part One — Read the first verse by heart twenty times. Read the second verse twenty times. Read the first and second together ten times to link them. Read the third verse twenty times, then the second and third together ten times. Read the fourth verse twenty times, then the third and fourth together ten times. Finally, read all four verses by heart ten times.

Part Two — Read the fifth verse by heart twenty times, then link the fourth and fifth ten times. Read the sixth twenty times, then link the fifth and sixth ten times. Read the seventh twenty times, then link the sixth and seventh ten times. Read the eighth twenty times, then link the seventh and eighth ten times.
Read from the fifth through the eighth verse by heart ten times to link the second half. Then read the entire page by heart ten times to master it.

Note — Do not restrict memorization to a complete verse, because a verse may be very long or very short. Memorize by the amount of one or two lines. Sūrat al-Jumuʿah is used as an example because each verse is approximately this length.
Twenty times for each new passage. Ten times to link each passage to the next.
Section Four: The Method of Reviewing the Previous Lesson
Before you memorize the new lesson, review by heart what you memorized in the previous five days, up to the place of the new lesson.
After that, begin memorizing the new lesson according to the repetition and linking method explained above.
Section Five: Combining Memorization and Review

Memorization does not take firm root except through review. Ibn al-Jawzī said that persistence is a great foundation, and many who abandoned review after memorizing spent a long time recovering what they had forgotten.
The ideal method is to combine memorizing the Qur'an and reviewing it at the same time.
1 — While memorizing from Sūrat al-Nās to al-Aḥqāf, review half a juzʾ every day from al-Nās until the place you are memorizing.
2 — From Sūrat al-Jāthiyah to al-ʿAnkabūt, review one juzʾ every day.
3 — From Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ to al-Kahf, review one and a half juzʾ every day.
4 — From Sūrat al-Isrāʾ to al-Tawbah, review two juzʾ every day.
5 — From Sūrat al-Anfāl to al-Māʾidah, review two and a half juzʾ every day.
6 — From Sūrat al-Nisāʾ to al-Baqarah, review three juzʾ every day.
After completing memorization of the Book of Allah together with its review, move to the stage of mastery explained in the next chapter.
Section Six: How Do I Distinguish Between Similar Verses?
If verses become confusingly similar, open the muṣḥaf to the similar verses, look at the difference between them, ponder them, and set a rule for yourself by which you distinguish between them.
During review, observe the difference between the similar verses repeatedly until you master the similarity between them.
The author notes that he devoted a separate book to the rules governing the similar verses of the Qur'an.
Chapter Four: The Easiest Method for Reviewing the Noble Qur'an
Section One: The Importance of Reviewing the Qur'an

1 — The Noble Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and His speech is not like human speech. If the memorizer does not review it, it slips away. The Prophet ﷺ said it escapes from people's breasts more quickly than camels from their ropes.
2 — Part of the wisdom of the Qur'an slipping from the hearts is that this motivates abundant recitation, so the servant may attain its reward.
3 — It is recommended to review the Noble Qur'an with a teacher, for that is firmer for what has been memorized. Al-Aʿmash said that he recited the Qur'an to Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb thirty times.
Keep refreshing your knowledge of the Qur'an, for it is more inclined to escape from men's breasts than camels from their ropes.
Section Two: The Method of Mastering the Qur'an
After memorizing and reviewing the whole Qur'an by the previous method, move on to the stage of mastery (itqān).
1 — Begin by reviewing the whole Qur'an from Sūrat al-Baqarah to Sūrat al-Nās.
2 — Read five juzʾ every day; by that you will complete the whole Qur'an every six days.
3 — Carry out this method for a full year.
By this method, within a year you will have mastered your memorization of the whole Qur'an—by the permission of Allah.
Five juzʾ each day. One complete Qur'an every six days. Continue for one year.
Section Three: In How Many Days Should You Complete the Qur'an?

After the mastery stage, move to a review cycle in which you complete the Qur'an by heart every week. The scholars gathered the weekly portions in the mnemonic “fa-mī bi-shawq”; each letter marks the beginning of a daily portion.
Day 1 — Fāʾ: from Sūrat al-Fātiḥah to the end of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.
Day 2 — Mīm: from Sūrat al-Māʾidah to the end of Sūrat al-Tawbah.
Day 3 — Yāʾ: from Sūrat Yūnus to the end of Sūrat al-Naḥl.
Day 4 — Bāʾ: from Sūrat Banī Isrāʾīl, also called al-Isrāʾ, to the end of Sūrat al-Furqān.
Day 5 — Shīn: from Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ to the end of Sūrat Yā-Sīn.
Day 6 — Wāw: from Sūrat wa-l-Ṣāffāt to the end of Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt.
Day 7 — Qāf: from Sūrat Qāf to the end of Sūrat al-Nās.
Chapter Five: The Isnād in the Noble Qur'an
Section One: The Importance of the Isnād in the Qur'an
The isnād in the Qur'an is presenting the complete Qur'an to a shaykh, while the shaykh presented it to his shaykh through a connected chain going back to the Prophet ﷺ.

Imam al-Suyūṭī said: “The ijāzah is like a testimony from the shaykh for the one granted it.” Ibn al-Jazarī said that recitation is an followed Sunnah, received by later generations from the earlier ones.
Among the fruits of ijāzah are three things:
1 — Receiving the Qur'an through a connected chain is among the means of preserving the Book of Allah, and this is among the distinctions granted to this nation.
2 — It is among the causes of precision in performance, mastery of transmission, and protection of the tongue from error.
3 — The person granted ijāzah attains the honor of entering the chain of those who preserve the Book of Allah by isnād.
Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it.
Section Two: Scholars Who Carry an Isnād in the Qur'an
The Salaf took learning the Qur'an as a foundation at the beginning of seeking knowledge. They received it by connected chains from their scholars, and those after them received it from them.

1–4 — Imam Abū Ḥanīfah (d. 150 AH) transmitted from al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Abī Laylā. Imam al-Layth ibn Saʿd (d. 175 AH) transmitted from Nāfiʿ. Imam Mālik (d. 179 AH) presented to Nāfiʿ ibn Abī Nuʿaym. Imam al-Shāfiʿī (d. 204 AH) presented to Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qusṭanṭīn.

5–8 — Al-Wāqidī (d. 207 AH) transmitted from Nāfiʿ, ʿĪsā ibn Wardān, and others. Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām (d. 224 AH) received by presentation and hearing from a large group including al-Kisāʾī. Yūnus al-Ṣadafī (d. 264 AH) recited to Warsh. Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī (d. 277 AH) transmitted variant readings by hearing.

9–12 — Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (d. 310 AH), author of the Tafsīr, received and taught variant readings and compiled a book on them. Ibn Khuzaymah (d. 311 AH) presented to ʿImrān al-Qazzāz. Al-Dāraquṭnī (d. 385 AH) taught recitation late in life and authored a distinguished work. Ibn Mandah (d. 395 AH) transmitted from teachers in Egypt and Baghdad.

13–16 — Al-Ḥākim al-Naysābūrī (d. 405 AH) presented to teachers across Khurasan, Baghdad, and Kūfah. Abū Nuʿaym al-Aṣbahānī (d. 430 AH) heard from al-Ṭabarānī. Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī (d. 444 AH) received multiple transmissions and taught a great multitude. Yūsuf al-Hudhalī (d. 465 AH) said he met 365 teachers in this science from the far west to Farghānah.

17–20 — Ibn ʿAqīl al-Ḥanbalī (d. 513 AH) recited to Ibn Shaytā. Al-Shāṭibī (d. 590 AH) became the leading teacher of recitation in Egypt and authored the celebrated Shāṭibiyyah. Ibn al-Ḥājib (d. 646 AH) received transmissions from al-Shāṭibī and others. Ibn Mālik (d. 672 AH), author of the Alfiyyah, took the recitations from Thābit ibn Khiyār.

21–24 — Ibrāhīm al-Fāḍilī (d. 692 AH) recited the Seven to al-Sakhāwī seven times. Abū Ḥayyān al-Andalusī (d. 745 AH) received and taught the Seven. Al-Dhahabī (d. 748 AH) devoted himself to the recitations from youth and traveled to study them. ʿAbd al-Raḥīm al-ʿIrāqī (d. 806 AH) recited the complete Seven.

25 — Ibn al-Jazarī (d. 833 AH) received from numerous shaykhs and taught in Makkah, Madinah, Cairo, Alexandria, Damascus, Basra, Bursa, Khurasan, Isfahan, Herat, Yazd, Shiraz, Samarkand, and beyond the river. He authored major works on the ten recitations.

26–28 — Zakariyyā al-Anṣārī (d. 926 AH) recited the Seven and the three additional recitations. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb (d. 1285 AH) recited to Ibrāhīm al-ʿUbaydī. ʿAbd al-Laṭīf ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (d. 1293 AH) recited the recitations to Salmūnah.
Section Three: Children Who Carry an Isnād in the Qur'an

Allah has made the recitation and memorization of the Qur'an easy for Muslims. Just as adults memorize it, so do children. Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad al-Aṣbahānī memorized the Qur'an at five years old, and children hastened to carry its isnād.

1 — ʿAbd al-Ṣamad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Andalusī al-Āshī transmitted the Qur'an from his father and heard several books from him while under ten. Abū Ḥayyān noted that people nevertheless narrated from him.

2 — Zayd ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Zayd al-Kindī al-Baghdādī recited the Qur'an by the ten transmissions at ten years old. Al-Dhahabī said this was something not prepared for anyone before him, and he lived until the highest chains in recitation and Hadith ended with him.
3 — ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ḥaḍramī recited the Qur'an to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Khazrajī and Niʿm al-Khalaf al-Anṣārī when he was ten.
4 — Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Mawṣilī, nicknamed Shuʿlah, recited the variant readings as a child to ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Irbilī.

5 — Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Ṣāʾigh recited to Ibn Nāshirah until Sūrat al-Fajr, but his teacher initially considered him too young for ijāzah. Al-Kamāl al-Ḍarīr interceded, saying: “We grant ijāzah to whoever crawls and walks; perhaps one of them will become noble, benefiting the people and being remembered.” Al-Ṣāʾigh later became the only person remaining who narrated from both teachers.

The author closes by asking Allah to grant us memorization of His Book with mastery, together with reflection upon it and acting by it, and sends prayers and peace upon the Prophet Muhammad, his family, and all his Companions.
